# Compositing

A composite combines many burst products into one image per grid square.
`ResolutionWeighter` writes composites on the 10 km squares of the MGRS grid,
so results from different bursts, orbits and dates line up pixel for pixel.

## Get the grid squares

`MGRSGrid` from [freezebase](https://github.com/lqgentner/freezebase) lists the
grid squares that overlap an area. Its `resolution` is the pixel size of the
composite and must equal the `grid_spacing` the products were processed with:

```{.python}
from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGrid
from shapely.geometry import box

aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))
```

Each square is an `MGRSGeoBox`, which knows its MGRS code, its pixel grid and
its UTM zone, `square.crs`. The products must be in that zone: process them
with `crs=square.crs` and keep the default `align_to_standard_grid=True`. A
product on a different grid is rejected with an `InconsistentInputsError` that
names it.

Do not process products for a composite with `crs="auto"`. That takes each
burst's own zone, and a burst whose centre lies in the neighbouring zone would
be projected there, not in the zone of the square.

## Compose backscatter

The main method, `compose_rtc_lrw()`, combines all RTC products that cover a
square, whatever their orbit or direction. Each pixel is weighted towards the
acquisitions that see it in the finest detail. This is called local resolution
weighting (LRW); [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains
how it works.

```{.python}
from s1bursts import ResolutionWeighter, TimeRange

weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
for square in squares:
    composite = weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(
        rtc.products, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window,
    )
```

The method returns the composite, a record whose file
`fm.get_product_path(composite)` holds the backscatter. Pass the `TimeRange` of
your search as `time_range`, so that every square records the same compositing
window.

## Quality layers

With `write_qa=True`, two quality layers are written beside the composite.
`QA-NUM` counts the acquisitions that contributed to each pixel, and `QA-CQM`
rates how fine the combined detail is. The composite lists them in its
`layers`, and `get_product_path()` locates each layer's file:

```{.python}
from s1bursts.product import Layer

num_path = fm.get_product_path(composite, Layer.QA_NUM)
cqm_path = fm.get_product_path(composite, Layer.QA_CQM)
```

## Other composites

Four more methods cover other inputs and groupings:

| Method | Combines | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `compose_coherence_lrw()` | Coherence, weighted like RTC | Coherence composites; also needs the RTC products of the same dates |
| `compose_rtc_by_pass()` | RTC, one composite per pass direction | Keeping ascending and descending orbits apart |
| `compose_gtc_by_pass()` | GTC, one composite per pass direction | Backscatter without terrain flattening |
| `compose_coherence_by_pass()` | Coherence, one composite per pass direction | Coherence by viewing direction |

The per-pass methods return a dictionary of composites keyed by pass direction,
`"Ascending"` and `"Descending"`. A direction that no product reaches is left
out. They take a plain average without resolution weights, and their only
quality layer is `QA-NUM`.

## Choose how to combine

Every method averages by default. Pass `aggregation="median"`, or a number
between 0 and 1 for a quantile, to reduce the influence of outliers.

Composites are written in linear units, like the products they combine.
Convert backscatter to decibels after reading it, as `10 * np.log10(gamma0)`,
so that the averaging has already happened on linear values.

All inputs of one composite must share a polarization, and coherence inputs
must share a temporal baseline.

## Errors in a loop over squares

A problem with the data of one square raises a `CompositeError` from
`s1bursts.errors`, so a loop over many squares can record it and move on:

| Error | Raised when |
|---|---|
| `EmptyCompositeError` | No product reaches the square; nothing is written |
| `InconsistentInputsError` | A product is in another UTM zone, pixel size or grid than the square, or the products were made with different DEMs |
| `CompositeInputError` | A product file is missing or cannot be read |

A wrong call, such as an empty list of products or mixed polarizations, raises
a plain `ValueError` instead, which `CompositeError` does not catch.

Like processing, compositing skips a square whose files already exist, after
checking that they were made on the same grid and with the same `aggregation`
and `clip_max_resolution`. Otherwise it raises a
`ProductSettingsMismatchError`. That error is not a `CompositeError`, because
every other square would meet it too. Pass `overwrite=True` to replace the old
composites.
